screens.title: The Pillars of Observability

This integrated approach ensures that all aspects of your system, from infrastructure to application logic, are transparent and manageable. Core Concept

The Pillars of Observability

Monitoring, Logging, and Alerting are essential for cloud-native applications.

Monitoring

Collecting quantitative data (metrics) about system performance and behavior.

Logging

Aggregating and analyzing event records generated by applications and infrastructure.

Alerting

Proactively notifying teams when predefined conditions or thresholds are breached.

Why it matters

Observability provides the visibility needed to understand system behavior, troubleshoot issues, and ensure reliability in complex, distributed environments like OpenShift.

Key Takeaway

Observability is not optional; it's the foundation for managing and maintaining healthy cloud-native applications on OpenShift.

screens.title: OpenShift Monitoring with Prometheus
screens.narratorSegment: OpenShift's monitoring capabilities are primarily driven by Prometheus, a powerful open-source time-series database and monitoring system. Prometheus works by 'scraping' metrics endpoints, which are essentially HTTP endpoints exposed by applications or OpenShift components that provide data in a specific format. It collects this data at regular intervals, storing it as time-series data. OpenShift automatically deploys and configures a Prometheus instance to scrape metrics from core cluster components, such as nodes, pods, and the control plane, giving you immediate insight into your infrastructure. For your own applications, the key is to ensure they expose metrics in the Prometheus format, typically on a slash metrics endpoint. This usually involves integrating a Prometheus client library into your application code. For example, a web server might expose metrics like request counts, latency, or error rates. Without Prometheus, you'd be manually checking each component, which is simply not scalable in a microservices architecture. The beauty of Prometheus is its pull-based model, where it actively fetches data, making it robust and efficient for dynamic environments. Remember, Prometheus is about collecting the raw data; visualization comes next.

keyIdea.title: Prometheus: Metric Collection
keyIdea.text: Prometheus is OpenShift's core metric collection system, scraping data from cluster components and applications.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Prometheus Monitoring
Monitoring Stack

OpenShift Monitoring with Prometheus

Prometheus collects metrics from applications and cluster components.

How Prometheus Works

  • •**Scraping:** Prometheus pulls metrics from configured HTTP endpoints.
  • •**Time-Series Database:** Stores metrics with timestamps for historical analysis.
  • •**Automatic Discovery:** OpenShift configures Prometheus to monitor core components.
  • •**Application Metrics:** Applications must expose metrics in Prometheus format (e.g., `/metrics`).
Example: Metrics Endpoint

A web application exposes `/metrics` with data like `http_requests_total{method="GET", path="/"} 1234`.

Prometheus in OpenShift

OpenShift integrates Prometheus to automatically monitor cluster components and allows for custom application metric collection.

Key Takeaway

Prometheus is the backbone of metric collection in OpenShift, providing raw data for performance analysis.

screens.title: Configuring Custom Metrics with ServiceMonitor
screens.narratorSegment: While OpenShift automatically monitors its core components, you'll need to explicitly tell Prometheus how to discover and scrape metrics from your custom applications. This is where the Service Monitor custom resource comes into play. A Service Monitor acts as a configuration for the Prometheus Operator, instructing it on which services to target, which ports to scrape, and at what interval. It's a powerful mechanism for extending OpenShift's monitoring capabilities to your specific application needs. For example, if your application exposes metrics on a named port, say 'metrics', and has a specific label like 'app=my-app', the Service Monitor will use these details to create the necessary scraping configuration for Prometheus. Without a Service Monitor, Prometheus wouldn't know where to look for your application's metrics, leaving a blind spot in your observability. It's crucial to ensure the labels in your Service Monitor match those on your application's Kubernetes Service definition. A common mistake is misconfiguring these labels, which prevents Prometheus from discovering your metrics. Always double-check your selectors and port names to ensure proper integration. This resource is fundamental for achieving comprehensive application-level monitoring.

keyIdea.title: ServiceMonitor for Discovery
keyIdea.text: A `ServiceMonitor` custom resource enables Prometheus to automatically discover and scrape application-specific metrics.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›ServiceMonitor
Custom Metrics

Configuring Custom Metrics with ServiceMonitor

Use ServiceMonitors to tell Prometheus how to scrape your application's metrics.

ServiceMonitor Explained

  • •**Custom Resource:** A Kubernetes object for Prometheus Operator.
  • •**Metric Discovery:** Defines how Prometheus finds application metrics endpoints.
  • •**Selector-Based:** Uses labels to match services for scraping.
  • •**Port & Interval:** Specifies the target port and scraping frequency.
Common Mistake

Mismatched labels in `ServiceMonitor` and Service definition will prevent Prometheus from discovering metrics.

ServiceMonitor Example

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: my-app-monitor
  labels:
    app: my-app
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app # Selects services with this label
  endpoints:
  - port: metrics # The name of the port in the Service definition
    interval: 30s
Key Takeaway

`ServiceMonitor` is crucial for extending OpenShift's monitoring to your custom application metrics.

screens.title: Visualizing Metrics with Grafana
screens.narratorSegment: Once Prometheus has collected your metrics, the next step is to make sense of that data. This is where Grafana comes in. Grafana is an open-source platform for data visualization, dashboarding, and alerting, and it's tightly integrated with OpenShift's monitoring stack. OpenShift typically includes a pre-configured Grafana instance that is already connected to the Prometheus data source. This means you can immediately start creating custom dashboards to visualize your application's performance, track resource utilization, and monitor business-specific Key Performance Indicators, or KPIs. Grafana allows you to build rich, interactive dashboards with various panel types, from graphs and single-value displays to heatmaps and tables. For example, you could create a dashboard showing HTTP request rates, error percentages, and C P U usage for your microservices. Architects should collaborate closely with development teams to identify the most critical metrics and design dashboards that provide actionable insights, not just raw data. The goal is to transform complex metric data into easily understandable visual representations that enable quick decision-making and troubleshooting. Without effective visualization, even the most comprehensive metric collection can be overwhelming and difficult to interpret. Grafana makes your data tell a story.

screens.title: OpenShift Logging with the EFK Stack
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond metrics, understanding the sequence of events within your applications and infrastructure is crucial, and that's where logging comes in. OpenShift provides a robust logging solution known as the EFK stack, which stands for Elasticsearch, Fluentd, and Kibana. Each component plays a distinct but integrated role. Fluentd runs as a DaemonSet on each node in your OpenShift cluster. Its job is to collect logs from various sources: containers, nodes, and OpenShift components themselves. It then forwards these logs to Elasticsearch. Elasticsearch acts as the central storage and indexing engine. It's a powerful search and analytics engine that makes your logs searchable and queryable at scale. Finally, Kibana provides a user-friendly web interface for visualizing and analyzing these logs. With Kibana, you can query, filter, and create dashboards from your log data, which is incredibly valuable for debugging, security auditing, and understanding application behavior. For example, if a microservice is experiencing errors, you can quickly search for error logs from that specific service in Kibana. This centralized approach eliminates the need to SSH into individual nodes or pods to inspect logs, significantly streamlining troubleshooting efforts. The EFK stack is a cornerstone of effective log management in OpenShift.

Logging Stack

OpenShift Logging with the EFK Stack

Centralized log aggregation and analysis using Elasticsearch, Fluentd, and Kibana.

Fluentd

Collects logs from containers and nodes, then forwards them.

Elasticsearch

Stores and indexes logs, making them searchable and queryable.

Kibana

screens.title: Structured Logging for Enhanced Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: While collecting logs is important, the format in which they are produced significantly impacts their usefulness. It's crucial for applications to produce structured logs, rather than just plain text. Structured logs, typically in JSON format, are machine-readable, making them much easier for Fluentd and Elasticsearch to parse and index. This enables far more powerful querying and analysis in Kibana. Imagine trying to search for all logs related to a specific user session if your logs are just free-form text; it would be incredibly difficult. With structured logs, you can include specific fields like a correlation underscore id, service name, or error underscore code, which then become searchable fields in Kibana. This allows you to quickly filter and correlate events across multiple microservices, drastically improving your debugging and troubleshooting capabilities. For instance, if a user reports an issue, you can use their correlation underscore id to trace their request across every service it touched. The Python example demonstrates how to implement structured logging, ensuring that each log entry is a valid JSON object. A common pitfall is sticking to plain text logs, which severely limits the analytical power of your EFK stack. Adopting structured logging is a critical best practice for any cloud-native application.

keyIdea.title: Structured Logs: Powering Analysis
keyIdea.text: Structured logging (e.g., JSON) makes logs machine-readable, enabling powerful querying and correlation in Kibana.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Structured Logging
Logging Best Practices

Structured Logging for Enhanced Analysis

Produce machine-readable logs for easier parsing and powerful querying.

Benefits of Structured Logging

  • •**Machine-Readable:** Easily parsed by Fluentd and Elasticsearch.
  • •**Powerful Querying:** Search by specific fields (e.g., `correlation_id`, `level`).
  • •**Improved Correlation:** Link related events across microservices.
  • •**Enhanced Debugging:** Faster identification of root causes.
Common Pitfall

Using plain text logs severely limits the ability to effectively query and analyze log data in Kibana.

Structured Logging Example (Python)

import logging
import json

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
handler = logging.StreamHandler()
formatter = logging.Formatter(json.dumps({
    "timestamp": "%(asctime)s",
    "level": "%(levelname)s",
    "message": "%(message)s",
    "service": "my-app",
    "correlation_id": "%(correlation_id)s" # Custom field
}))
handler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.addHandler(handler)

# Example usage
logger.info("User logged in successfully", extra={"correlation_id": "abc-123"})
logger.error("Database connection failed", extra={"correlation_id": "def-456", "error_code": 500})
Key Takeaway

Structured logs enable advanced querying and correlation, making log analysis significantly more effective in OpenShift.

screens.title: Proactive Alerting with Alertmanager
screens.narratorSegment: While monitoring and logging provide visibility into your system's state, alerting is the proactive component of observability. It ensures that operations teams are notified immediately when critical issues arise, allowing for rapid response and mitigation. OpenShift's monitoring stack integrates seamlessly with Alertmanager, which is designed to handle alerts sent by client applications like Prometheus. Alertmanager doesn't just forward every alert; it intelligently deduplicates, groups, and routes them to various notification channels. This is crucial for preventing 'alert fatigue,' where teams are overwhelmed by a flood of individual alerts. For example, if multiple pods of a single application start failing simultaneously, Alertmanager can group these related alerts into a single notification, providing a clearer picture of the overall incident. You define these alerting rules directly in Prometheus, using its powerful query language, PromQL. Alertmanager can then send notifications via email, Slack, PagerDuty, or custom webhooks, ensuring your team receives alerts through their preferred communication channels. The goal is to get the right information to the right people at the right time, enabling proactive issue detection and minimizing downtime. Without effective alerting, even well-monitored systems can suffer from delayed responses to critical problems.

Proactive Alerting with Alertmanager

Alertmanager handles, groups, and routes alerts from Prometheus to various channels.

Alertmanager Capabilities

  • •**Grouping:** Combines similar alerts into a single notification.
  • •**Routing:** Sends alerts to specific teams or channels (email, Slack, PagerDuty).

Multiple pods failing for one application trigger a single, grouped alert to the responsible team via Slack.

→→

Prometheus detects an issue, sends an alert to Alertmanager, which then routes it to the appropriate notification channel.

Alertmanager is critical for managing and routing alerts, ensuring timely and effective incident response in OpenShift.

screens.title: Defining Prometheus Alerting Rules
screens.narratorSegment: To make Alertmanager effective, you need to define clear alerting rules within Prometheus. These rules are based on PromQL, Prometheus's powerful query language, which allows you to define conditions that, when met, trigger an alert. An alerting rule typically consists of an expression, a duration, labels, and annotations. The expression is a PromQL query that evaluates to a set of time series. The for clause specifies how long the condition must be true before an alert is fired, preventing transient issues from triggering unnecessary notifications. Labels provide metadata about the alert, such as severity, while annotations offer human-readable summaries and descriptions. For instance, you might define a rule to alert if the 5xx error rate for your application exceeds 5% for a continuous period of 5 minutes. This ensures that only persistent, significant issues generate alerts. Architects should work to define clear Service Level Objectives, or SLOs, and Service Level Indicators, or SLIs, to drive these alerting rules. This ensures that alerts are not only actionable but also directly tied to the performance and reliability goals of your services. Without well-defined rules, alerts can be either missed or become a source of 'noise,' leading to alert fatigue. Testing these rules is also paramount to ensure they fire correctly when needed.

content.html:
Module X›Chapter Y›Prometheus Rules
Alerting Rules

Defining Prometheus Alerting Rules

Use PromQL to create rules that trigger alerts based on metric thresholds.

Components of an Alert Rule

  • •**`alert`:** Unique name for the alert.
  • •**`expr`:** PromQL query defining the alerting condition.
  • •**`for`:** Duration the condition must be true before firing.
  • •**`labels`:** Key-value pairs for alert metadata (e.g., severity).
  • •**`annotations`:** Human-readable information (summary, description).
SLO/SLI Connection

Alerting rules should be driven by defined Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and Service Level Indicators (SLIs) for actionable alerts.

Prometheus Alerting Rule Example

# rules.yaml
groups:
- name: application-alerts
  rules:
  - alert: HighErrorRate
    expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="my-app", status_code=~"5xx"}[5m])) by (app) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="my-app"}[5m])) by (app) > 0.05
    for: 5m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: "High error rate detected for {{ $labels.app }}"
      description: "{{ $labels.app }} is experiencing a 5xx error rate above 5% for 5 minutes."
Key Takeaway

Prometheus alerting rules, powered by PromQL, enable precise and actionable notifications based on defined thresholds.

screens.title: Common Observability Mistakes & Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: As you implement observability in OpenShift, it's important to be aware of common mistakes and adopt best practices to ensure your strategy is effective and secure. One frequent pitfall is collecting too many metrics or logs without a clear purpose. This leads to 'observability noise,' where valuable signals are drowned out by irrelevant data, and it also increases storage costs. The key is to focus on metrics and logs that are truly indicative of application health, performance, and business value. Another critical mistake is neglecting to test your alerting rules. An alert that doesn't fire when it should, or fires too often, is worse than no alert at all, as it erodes trust and leads to alert fatigue. Always validate your rules in a non-production environment. From a security perspective, it's crucial to ensure sensitive information, such as passwords or Personally Identifiable Information, is never logged. Implement proper log sanitization and redaction. Furthermore, access to monitoring and logging dashboards must be properly controlled via Role-Based Access Control, or RBAC, to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive operational data. By avoiding these common errors and adhering to best practices, you can build a robust, efficient, and secure observability strategy for your OpenShift environments. Remember, observability is an ongoing process that requires continuous refinement.

Operational Excellence

Common Observability Mistakes & Best Practices

Avoid pitfalls and ensure your observability strategy is effective and secure.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • •**Observability Noise:** Collecting too many irrelevant metrics or logs.
  • •**Untested Alerts:** Alerts that don't fire or fire too often, leading to fatigue.
  • •**Neglecting Security:** Logging sensitive data or inadequate access control.
Impact

These mistakes can lead to increased costs, delayed incident response, and security vulnerabilities.

Best Practices for Success

  • •**Purpose-Driven Data:** Focus on metrics and logs that provide actionable insights.
  • •**Test Alerting Rules:** Regularly validate that alerts fire correctly.
  • •**Structured & Sanitized Logs:** Implement structured logging and redact sensitive information.
  • •**RBAC for Dashboards:** Control access to monitoring and logging tools.
Key Takeaway

A well-designed observability strategy is purpose-driven, thoroughly tested, and secure, providing true value to operations.

OpenShift's monitoring capabilities are primarily driven by Prometheus, a powerful open-source time-series database and monitoring system. Prometheus works by 'scraping' metrics endpoints, which are essentially HTTP endpoints exposed by applications or OpenShift components that provide data in a specific format. It collects this data at regular intervals, storing it as time-series data. OpenShift automatically deploys and configures a Prometheus instance to scrape metrics from core cluster components, such as nodes, pods, and the control plane, giving you immediate insight into your infrastructure. For your own applications, the key is to ensure they expose metrics in the Prometheus format, typically on a slash metrics endpoint. This usually involves integrating a Prometheus client library into your application code. For example, a web server might expose metrics like request counts, latency, or error rates. Without Prometheus, you'd be manually checking each component, which is simply not scalable in a microservices architecture. The beauty of Prometheus is its pull-based model, where it actively fetches data, making it robust and efficient for dynamic environments. Remember, Prometheus is about collecting the raw data; visualization comes next.

While OpenShift automatically monitors its core components, you'll need to explicitly tell Prometheus how to discover and scrape metrics from your custom applications. This is where the Service Monitor custom resource comes into play. A Service Monitor acts as a configuration for the Prometheus Operator, instructing it on which services to target, which ports to scrape, and at what interval. It's a powerful mechanism for extending OpenShift's monitoring capabilities to your specific application needs. For example, if your application exposes metrics on a named port, say 'metrics', and has a specific label like 'app=my-app', the Service Monitor will use these details to create the necessary scraping configuration for Prometheus. The goal is to transform complex metric data into easily understandable visual representations that enable quick decision-making and troubleshooting. It's crucial for applications to produce structured logs, rather than just plain text. This allows you to quickly filter and correlate events across multiple microservices, drastically improving your debugging and troubleshooting capabilities. For instance, if a user reports an issue, you can use their correlation underscore id to trace their request across every service it touched.
